notes: Full cross-appeal judgment on contract construction and split-trial costs discretion.

enrichment.short_title: Signed consultancy letter held to be immediate binding contract; split-trial liability costs may be deferred
key_facts: Mr Weill, a financial consultant, exchanged a signed letter dated 19 August 1999 with Mean Fiddler Holdings setting out consultancy fees, expenses and share warrants after prolonged negotiations.
At trial on liability only, HHJ Bruce Coles QC held the signed document was a binding contract and rejected the defendant's case that it had been discharged.
The defendant appealed on construction; the claimant cross-appealed because the judge reserved costs of the liability trial until after the damages trial.
The defendant argued the closing sentence about 'formalising our relationship under contract' showed no immediate contract was intended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a split trial on liability in a claim for specific performance or damages for breach of consultancy agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed with costs; defendant's construction appeal failed and claimant's immediate costs order refused.
enrichment.ratio: Viewed in its factual matrix, a signed stand-alone letter setting out complete remuneration terms and accepted by the defendant's managing director manifested an immediate binding contract rather than a non-contractual memorandum; on costs, a trial judge may defer an order on liability-trial costs where there is a real possibility that the outcome on quantum (including whether damages would be nominal) may affect entitlement to those costs.
legal_issues: Whether the signed letter of 19 August 1999 constituted an immediately binding contract
Whether the judge wrongly exercised his discretion in reserving costs of the liability trial

statutes_considered.title: Employment Tribunals (Constitution and Rules of Procedure) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Mrs Sheridan resigned after a final written warning following a workplace incident and succeeded in an unfair constructive dismissal claim before the Nottingham Employment Tribunal.
The employer's review application under rule 13 failed; at the review hearing the chairman relied on Deria and Lindsay without inviting submissions, though he had highlighted copies of those cases.
Dr Cohen, a director appearing in person for the employer, had not appealed the rule 13(1)(d) finding that Butlins employment evidence was not new.

enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal cites an authority that is relevant, significant and central to its decision but not argued by the parties, it should normally refer it to the parties; however failure to do so is not necessarily a serious procedural irregularity unless the party shows material injustice, meaning reasonably arguable submissions could have produced a different result.

Whether centrality of an authority alone suffices or material injustice must also be shown
Whether Deria and Lindsay were central to refusing review under rule 13(1)(e)

enrichment.short_title: Claimant may pursue solicitor negligence despite Coutts fraud finding; strike-out reversed
key_facts: Mr Sweetman bought moorland using Coutts loans, was deceived about purchaser Darvist versus shell company Darvis, and obtained summary judgment against him and Nathan's partners for defrauding Coutts over a £1.5M second loan.
Assigned from his trustee in bankruptcy, he sued Nathan's partners for negligent failure to warn of the Darvis substitution and related losses, including £441,000 retained by Nathan.
Stanley Burnton J struck out the claim for issue estoppel and abuse of process; the Court of Appeal in related Shepherds proceedings had allowed a deceit claim to continue on conditions.
The court declined to follow the earlier concession that a fraud finding necessarily barred recovery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from strike-out of professional negligence claim against solicitor partners as assignee of trustee causes of action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; strike-out set aside; claimant ordered to give security for defendants' costs; issue estoppel and abuse of process left for trial.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant's action against a solicitor for negligent conveyancing can be pleaded and proved without reliance on the claimant's own fraud on a bank; ex turpi causa does not automatically bar recovery where the unlawful conduct is incidental rather than the direct foundation of the claim, following Standard Chartered Bank (No 2); Munni Bibi issue estoppel conditions were not satisfied between co-defendants in the earlier Coutts proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether a prior fraud finding estopped the claimant from suing Nathan's partners
Whether relitigation amounted to abuse of process under Johnson v Gore Wood
Whether ex turpi causa barred the negligence claim
Whether the £441,000 trust claim could proceed independently

notes: Complete costs appeal on construction of consent order for claim and counterclaim costs.

enrichment.short_title: Consent order 'costs of the action' construed to include counterclaim defence costs
key_facts: Alpacas Ltd claimed £14,687.50 for unpaid invoices; Wilsey counterclaimed for £24,234.37 commission and the matter settled by consent order dated 7 May 2002.
The defendant paid £8,000 damages, withdrew the counterclaim, and was ordered to pay the claimant's 'costs of the action' on the standard basis.
Costs Officer Baker held the phrase excluded counterclaim costs and applied CPR 44.4(2) to resolve ambiguity against the paying party.
Settlement correspondence used 'action' and 'matter' in a broad sense covering both claim and counterclaim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to a High Court judge from an authorised costs officer's preliminary decision on the scope of a consent costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; costs officer's directions rescinded; 'costs of the action' held to include costs of defending the counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: On ordinary principles of contractual interpretation (Investors Compensation Scheme), 'costs of the action' in a consent order settling both claim and withdrawn counterclaim, read with the schedule and antecedent correspondence, would convey to a reasonable person that all litigation costs including counterclaim costs were intended; CPR 44.4(2) applies to reasonableness of costs incurred, not to construction of an order; Atlas Metal is distinguishable on post-judgment versus consensual settlement facts.
legal_issues: Whether 'costs of the action' in a consent order includes counterclaim costs
Whether CPR 44.4(2) governs interpretation of consent orders
Whether Atlas Metal Company v Miller applies

enrichment.short_title: Court of Appeal guidance on civil restraint orders and two-year extended order against Bhamjee
key_facts: Mr Bhamjee had made numerous hopeless permission-to-appeal and judicial review applications, imposing heavy cost on court resources while respondents were often not vexed because permission was refused.
Following Bhamjee (No 1), a three-judge court considered protective measures; five barrister respondents also sought an extended Grepe v Loam order.
The court reviewed vexatious litigation, section 42 civil proceedings orders, Grepe v Loam orders, and Ebert v Venvil extended orders.
Mr Bhamjee threatened further proceedings against lawyers and showed no acceptance of prior refusals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second judgment of the Court of Appeal following dismissal of permission applications in Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 1), considering systemic remedies and respondents' injunction application.
enrichment.outcome: Extended civil restraint order made for two years against Mr Bhamjee in relation to the five barrister defendants, with paper permission procedure via Master Bowman and appeal to Park J.
enrichment.ratio: Courts have inherent jurisdiction proportionate to abuse of process to restrain hopeless litigation that wastes judicial resources; a graduated scheme applies—civil restraint orders for single proceedings, extended civil restraint orders (up to two years) for persistent vexatious conduct across related litigation, and general civil restraint orders where wider protection is needed—provided Article 6 access is not extinguished.
legal_issues: Whether waste of court resources alone justifies injunctive restraint
The interface between section 42 orders and inherent Grepe v Loam jurisdiction
What form of extended civil restraint order was appropriate against Mr Bhamjee

notes: Full pension negligence appeal applying Scally implied term analysis.

enrichment.short_title: No Scally duty to inform bus driver of enhanced pension transfer option on privatisation
key_facts: Mr Ibekwe, an LTE/London General bus driver, lost enhanced ill-health pension rights after MEBO privatisation in November 1994 because he did not transfer accrued LRT scheme benefits to the new LG scheme before dismissal in January 1995.
Preliminary issues asked whether LG owed a duty to inform him of the enhanced transfer option, whether it was breached, and whether breach caused his failure to transfer.
The judge found Mr Ibekwe received October and November 1994 letters but not the December 1994 letter enclosing the transfer form.
LG conceded that with a successful enhanced transfer Mr Ibekwe would have fared better on ill-health retirement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Bow County Court dismissal after trial of preliminary issues in pension misinformation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no Scally-type implied duty found and reasonable steps taken in any event; tort duty not fair, just and reasonable.
enrichment.ratio: The Scally implied term applies only where pension rights are incorporated into contracts negotiated with a representative body and confer a valuable contingent option of which the employee cannot reasonably be expected to be aware; MEBO transfer terms negotiated between seller and purchaser did not satisfy that category; where an employer tells an employee no action is needed until further information is sent, reasonable steps require sending that follow-up information.
legal_issues: Whether Scally implied a duty to inform of enhanced pension transfer on privatisation
Whether LG took reasonable steps to communicate pension options
Whether a parallel tort duty of care arose
Causation if trustees refused post-dismissal transfer

enrichment.short_title: Two non-adjoining houses may be one dwelling for jobseeker's allowance capital disregard

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mr Miah, with a large family, owned two three-bedroom houses two doors apart on Haseley Road, Handsworth; occupying only one would cause statutory overcrowding.
Income-based jobseeker's allowance disregards capital in one 'dwelling occupied as the home'; capital over £8,000 disqualified him after redundancy.
The Commissioner held a dwelling could comprise more than one building and remitted the case; a rehearing tribunal found both houses formed a single split-site home.
The Secretary of State appealed, arguing only one physical building could be disregarded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission from the Social Security Commissioner against construction of Jobseeker's Allowance capital disregard rules.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; matter remitted on Commissioner's basis that two buildings may constitute one dwelling if functionally a single home.
enrichment.ratio: Although Schedule 8 paragraph 1 limits disregard to one dwelling and prevents disregarding a partner's separate home, 'dwelling occupied as the home' in regulation 1(3) focuses on the functional home normally occupied by the claimant and can exceptionally comprise more than one building where arrangements show a single split-site home (annex test), rather than two wholly separate residences.
legal_issues: Whether two separate houses can amount to one dwelling for Schedule 8 capital disregard
The effect of regulation 88 and 'only one dwelling' wording
Comparison with income support and supplementary benefit definitions

notes: Complete compulsory purchase compensation appeal on estoppel and valuation date.

enrichment.short_title: Subject-to-contract settlement offer cannot estop acquiring authority from adducing valuation evidence
key_facts: The Secretary of State compulsorily acquired Mr and Mrs Christos's Detling property (house plus 35 acres) for the Channel Tunnel Rail Link.
Mr Bowman offered £500,000 subject to contract to buy the whole property; the claimants accepted subject to contract but no formal contracts were exchanged.
The parties agreed valuation date 17 May 1999 when partial entry occurred; the house later suffered £8,500 water damage before full possession.
The Lands Tribunal valued the land at £485,000 using estoppel to fix open-market value at £500,000 less £15,000 for defective title to adversely possessed woodland.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from Lands Tribunal compensation determination; cross-appeal on binding contract, main appeal on estoppel and post-valuation damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on estoppel; cross-appeal dismissed on contract; remitted for re-determination without estoppel bar; no deduction for post-valuation-date damage.
enrichment.ratio: An offer to settle compulsory purchase compensation marked subject to contract does not become a binding agreement or a representation of value capable of estoppel; where parties agree a single valuation date, compensation is assessed by reference to the property's condition on that date, not subsequent deterioration while claimants remained in occupation.
legal_issues: Whether subject-to-contract acceptance created a binding £500,000 contract
Whether equitable estoppel prevented the authority from adducing valuation evidence below £500,000
Whether £8,500 post-valuation water damage should reduce compensation

notes: Full workplace stress appeal applying Hatton foreseeability and breach analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Employer not liable where only future stress risk was foreseeable, not immediate breakdown
key_facts: Miss Pratley, a Surrey County Council care manager, developed depression after returning from holiday in September 1996 when promised case 'stacking' had not been implemented.
She had hidden extensive unrecorded overtime and downplayed stress before an August 1996 supervision note recorded fears for future health if workload continued.
The judge found failure to introduce stacking materially caused her illness but that Mrs Elrick reasonably deferred action until after holiday.
Psychiatric evidence treated loss of the 'cherished idea' of stacking as a triggering life event.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Buckley J's dismissal of employer negligence claim for psychiatric injury caused by workplace stress.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; no breach of duty found.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Hatton, liability for stress-related psychiatric injury requires foreseeable risk of the particular harm suffered; where an employer foresees only a future risk of illness if workload is not reorganised, it is not negligent to defer steps until the employee returns from holiday, and breach in relation to that future risk cannot ground liability for an immediate breakdown caused by a different mechanism unless that immediate risk was itself foreseeable.
legal_issues: Foreseeability of psychiatric injury from workplace stress
Whether agreed stacking should have been implemented before claimant's return
Distinction between future overload risk and immediate collapse on return
Causation and remoteness under Hatton and Jolley
